summary: Closing update, with the run nearly out of time and every established finding already recorded. One source rule that the shift's condition depends on was still undocumented, so I read it out of the leader's re-synchronisation path and recorded it: whether a follower's accepted entries survive is decided from the promise metadata, not its log length — a follower that accepted in the same round as the most up-to-date promise the leader adopted keeps only up to the smaller accepted index, and everything after that is replaced by the leader's log. In the violating runs the origin carried that same accepted round but a longer accepted index (its two buffered entries), so the common accepted index was the adopted promise's zero and both entries were replaced — exactly the precondition the stale placeholders need — while in the decoupling run, where the follower flushed quickly, they fell inside the common prefix and survived. That makes the flush deadline's role concrete end to end: the flush deadline decides how far the adopted promise has progressed, this rule decides whether the origin's entries are replaced, and the placeholder accounting decides what index the later caller is told. I added that as knowledge with its anchors and left the missing 2×2 cell (a small tick with a fast flush) as the discriminator rather than opening another construction with minutes left; no execution was requested (validation reports execution_requested false). The run's record now holds three asserted defects — the actor layer's false `Ok` for a lost entry with its measured condition, the core's trim path unable to compact when the largest node id exceeds the node count, and the shifted index reported for a later caller under the original batching configuration — plus two bounded negatives on reordering and on duplication with stale-leader replay.
